opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is really the heart of what we were looking at. The intuition is fairly simple once you write it down. Suppose the model's per-token behavior is improving smoothly as you scale: more parameters, more compute, and the probability of getting any individual token right creeps up gradually and predictably. That's roughly what you'd expect from the scaling-law literature, where cross-entropy loss falls off nicely as a power law.

Now suppose your metric is exact match, where the model only gets credit if every one of, say, L tokens in the answer is correct. Approximately, the chance of getting the whole sequence right is the per-token accuracy raised to the power L. That exponent does a lot of work. If per-token accuracy goes from 0.8 to 0.9 to 0.95, and your answer is ten or twenty tokens long, the sequence-level accuracy sits near zero for a long stretch and then shoots up over a fairly narrow range of scale. When you plot that against model size, especially on a log axis, it looks like a sharp, unpredictable jump. It looks like a phase transition, like the model suddenly "gets" something.

But nothing discontinuous happened in the model. The underlying capability improved smoothly the whole time. The sharpness comes from the nonlinearity of the metric, this all-or-nothing scoring. That's why we argued that many claims of emergence are, at least in part, a property of the researcher's choice of measurement rather than a fundamental change in model behavior.

There are a couple of ways we tested this. One was to take the same model outputs and score them with something continuous or linear, like token edit distance or Brier score instead of exact match, or multiple-choice grade. When you do that, a lot of these dramatic jumps become smooth, predictable curves. Another was to go the other way: take tasks nobody considers emergent, including vision models, and deliberately pick a harsh, discontinuous metric, and you can manufacture what looks like emergence.

There's also a statistical piece. With exact match at small scales, nearly everything scores zero, and with limited test sets you can't resolve the difference between, say, 0.001 percent and 0.01 percent accuracy. Everything looks flat until it doesn't. With enough evaluation data, or a more sensitive metric, you often see that the smaller models were above chance and improving all along.

I want to be careful about the claim, though. We're not saying models never acquire qualitatively new behaviors, or that sharp transitions are impossible. And exact match isn't a bad metric. Sometimes you really do care whether the whole answer is right, like when code has to compile or arithmetic has to be exact. The point is that if you want to argue a model has an emergent ability, you need to rule out the explanation that your metric is creating the sharpness. And practically, this is good news: if improvement is actually smooth under the hood, then capabilities are more predictable than the emergence story suggests, which matters a lot for planning and for safety.

r001.rationale: It says per-token accuracy improves smoothly and whole-sequence accuracy is approximately that accuracy raised to the sequence length, so sequence accuracy rises from near zero before shooting up through the apparent transition.

r002.rationale: It explains that a higher per-token chance of correctness raises the chance that the entire sequence is correct, even though exact-match scoring is all-or-nothing.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the core of the argument we made in the "Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?" paper. The way I like to think about it is to start from what we actually know about scaling. If you look at the raw quantity that these models are trained to optimize, which is roughly the per-token cross-entropy, that improves smoothly and predictably as you scale up. There's no sharp transition there. So the question is: how do you get from a smooth, gradual improvement in per-token accuracy to a curve that looks flat, flat, flat, and then suddenly jumps?

And the answer turns out to be pretty mechanical once you look at the metric. Take something like multi-step arithmetic, or any task where the model has to produce a sequence of tokens and you only give credit if every single token is correct. If the model's probability of getting any individual token right is p, and the answer has L tokens, then under a rough independence assumption the probability of getting the whole thing right is p to the power L. That's an exponential function of per-token accuracy. So when p is, say, 0.8 and L is ten, you're at about ten percent. When p is 0.9, you're at thirty-something percent. When p is 0.99, you're close to ninety. The underlying improvement in p is smooth and roughly linear in log scale, but the exact-match score sits near zero for a long time and then climbs very steeply right at the end. That's exactly the hockey-stick shape people point to as evidence of emergence.

So the shape isn't telling you something fundamental changed inside the model. It's telling you that you chose a scoring rule that is nonlinear and, specifically, discontinuous in the thing that's actually improving. The model doesn't get partial credit for getting nine of ten digits right, even though in terms of capability that's a huge step forward from getting five of ten.

The test of that hypothesis is straightforward. If you take the same models, same outputs, and swap in a metric that gives partial credit, like token edit distance, the sharp transitions go away. You get smooth, continuous improvement with scale. Or you can go the other direction: take a task where everyone agrees there's nothing emergent, like a vision model classifying images, apply an all-or-nothing metric, and you can manufacture emergence that nobody would have claimed was there.

There's a second ingredient too, which is resolution. A lot of the benchmarks where emergence was claimed have pretty small test sets. If the true probability of success is one percent and you have a hundred examples, you're going to see zero most of the time. Then at the next model size you see a handful of successes, and that reads as "the ability appeared." But that's a sampling artifact, not a capability artifact. Once you increase the number of test examples and look at the small models carefully, you see they're above zero and improving, just in a region where the metric has very poor resolution.

I want to be careful about what we're not saying. We're not saying models don't get better with scale, obviously they do, and we're not saying it's impossible for some genuinely discontinuous capability to exist. What we're saying is that the specific evidence usually presented, the sharp curves on exact-match metrics, is fully explained by the choice of metric and the test set size. So if someone wants to claim emergence, the burden is on them to show it survives a continuous metric and adequate statistical resolution. And in the cases we looked at, it generally doesn't.

r001.rationale: The response says exact-match scores remain near zero and then rise steeply as per-token accuracy improves, and that small models are already above zero and improving below the apparent transition.

r002.rationale: It explains that whole-sequence accuracy is approximately p^L: increasing per-token correctness raises the chance of a fully correct sequence even though no partial credit is given.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to separate what’s happening with the model from what’s happening with the metric. If you only give credit when an entire sequence is correct, you’re imposing a very strict threshold on what might be fairly gradual improvements.

As a simple illustration, suppose each token is correct with probability p, and pretend those events are independent. For a sequence of length n, the probability of getting everything right is p to the n. So token-level performance can improve smoothly while sequence-level accuracy stays very low for a long time and then rises sharply. With a finite set of examples, that can look like the model suddenly acquired a capability.

The independence assumption isn’t realistic, but it illustrates the mechanism. The sharpness of the curve can come from how you measure success. Exact-match accuracy can be useful if your application really needs the whole answer to be correct. But that curve alone doesn’t establish that the underlying capability emerged discontinuously. You’d want to look at more granular measures as well.

r001.rationale: The response says sequence accuracy is pⁿ: it stays low as token accuracy improves, then rises sharply, so it increases through the apparent transition and below it.

r002.rationale: It explains that smoothly increasing per-token correctness raises the probability that an entire sequence is correct, even though scoring gives credit only for a fully correct sequence.

sol-6.1.text:
The key distinction is between the model improving and the metric we use to observe that improvement. If you score an answer as correct only when the entire token sequence is right, you’re applying a very sharp threshold. Getting almost everything right earns the same score as getting everything wrong.

For intuition, suppose each token is correct with probability p. Under a simplifying independence assumption, the probability of getting a sequence of length n entirely correct is p to the n. So even if token-level performance improves smoothly, exact-match performance can stay very low for a while and then rise sharply. That can look like an ability suddenly emerging.

That doesn’t mean the improvement isn’t real. It means the shape of that curve alone doesn’t establish a discontinuous change in the model’s capabilities. You need to look at more granular measures and ask whether the apparent emergence persists when you change how you score the task.

r001.rationale: The response says exact-match performance stays low and then rises sharply as token-level performance improves smoothly; its pⁿ example conveys that exact-sequence accuracy increases even below the apparent transition.

r002.rationale: The response explains that improving per-token correctness raises the probability pⁿ of an entirely correct sequence, despite scoring each sequence only as wholly correct or incorrect.
